Its easy to learn, extreamly hard to master (more so than chess).

With chess the first piece moved can't be in that many combinations. The first move has 19^2 combinations in go. Each piece in chess has a range of value, but it doesn't matter much how many pieces you loose, you only new 2 pieces to get a check mate in win. In Go each piece is worth the same, and its value is completly dependant on placement, and the pieces around it. The very minimal amount of pieces needed to create an uncapturable structure is 6 pieces (and that requires you to be wedged in a corner). Although uncapturable that only gains you 2 points. So while you can have uncapturable structures semi easily, its even more work to make structures unable to be devalued in play.

There is no end of the game until the board is litterally full and both players agree to end the game. At which point the winner is calculated with the largest (Area in control - captured pieces). Meaning you might have made uncapturable and un devaluable structures, but you can still lose if the other player captured enough of your pieces. In fact you could control 100 squares of area in the game, and the other player 1, and he could still win.

and thats just one senario. Just like chess has tips and tricks on what to do with certain piece combos, Go has hundreds if not thousands of stratagies for commonly found patterns.

And this is just "basics". at most you need 4 pieces to capture one piece, at least 2. The way you control area ranges from very sloppy, to ok, to tight, and you all have to plan a head on what to do from structure to structure, on the fly.
